content: Brainwashing, as a mechanism by which groups convert people against their will, was examined and rejected by the sociology of religion before this essay was written. Barker's study of the Unification Church, the paradigm case, found that fewer than ten percent of those who attended recruitment workshops joined, that most who joined left within two years, and that recruits were not the vulnerable and isolated of the popular account (Barker 1984, The Making of a Moonie, book, no DOI); the American Psychological Association declined in 1987 to endorse the report that would have made coercive persuasion an accepted scientific construct, and the courts followed. Sleep deprivation, confession sessions and financial control occur in some groups and are harmful; what they do not do is override choice. The essay's list of horrors is the popular cult stereotype, and the essay then spends its length arguing that the popular cult stereotype is a bad guide to thinking about groups, which is right, and applies to the list.

quote: The word “cult” isn’t being used to symbolize rationality errors, it’s being used as a label for something that seems weird.
content: This is correct, and it is the sociologists' definition. The church–sect–cult typology classifies religious groups by their degree of tension with the surrounding society, so that "cult" names novelty and deviance relative to the mainstream rather than any internal property (Stark & Bainbridge 1985, The Future of Religion, book, no DOI). The essay treats this as a scandal about lay usage; it is the technical usage too, and the field adopted it because the internal properties the essay would prefer to classify by, thought control, exploitation, closure, do not sort groups cleanly and are found across the mainstream. What the essay adds is the observation that weirdness is a risk factor rather than a disease, which the typology also accepts. Where the essay overreaches is in treating the base-rate reasoning behind the nervousness as mere fear of dissent: new high-commitment groups with charismatic founders and total worldviews have a worse track record than political rallies, and a Bayesian who applies the extra burden of proof to weirdness, as the essay concedes one should, is not thereby confusing a heuristic with a phobia.

quote: These people can see at a glance that Singularitarianism is obviously not a full-blown cult with sleep deprivation etc.
content: The essay's own risk analysis, that the movement has the risk factors and needs constant effort, was more accurate than its reassurance. In the years since, groups within and adjacent to the movement this book founded have been the subject of accounts by former members and journalists describing communal isolation, leader-centering, punishment of dissent and, in at least one offshoot, deaths; the community itself produced post-mortems on these episodes in the vocabulary of these essays. This is not offered as a charge against a 2007 essay, which explicitly predicted the risk. It is offered against the essay's sixth complaint, that being asked "is this a cult?" is an annoying Catch-22 that places the answerer in the position of defending. The people asking were applying the essay's own base-rate reasoning to the essay's own movement, and on the record since, the question was worth asking. The annoyance the essay reports is the feeling of being the subject of the analysis rather than its author.
